lessons.title: Preparing and carrying out welding repairs
lessons.html:
Planning a weld repair

Farm implements crack and break: plough frames, disc harrow gangs, slasher decks, trailer drawbars and loader brackets. A good weld repair restores strength; a bad one fails in the land and can cause an accident. Before welding, decide whether the part should be welded at all. Safety-critical parts such as ROPS frames, steering parts and some hitch components must not be welded; replace them and follow the manufacturer's instructions.

Preparation

  1. Identify the metal: mild steel, high-strength steel, cast iron or aluminium each need different methods and filler. Ask the supervisor if unsure.
  2. Clean to bright metal with a grinder: remove paint, rust, oil and galvanising.
  3. For cracks, drill a small stop hole at each end, then grind a V-groove along the crack.
  4. For butt joints on thick plate, bevel the edges.
  5. Clamp or tack the parts in position to control distortion.
  6. If welding on the tractor, disconnect the battery and clamp the earth close to the weld.

Setting up arc welding

Choose the electrode type and diameter for the material and thickness, and set current within the electrode maker's range. Test on scrap of the same thickness first. For MIG, set wire speed and voltage from the machine chart and check gas flow.

Technique

  • Hold a short, steady arc and even travel speed.
  • Keep the right electrode angle for the joint and position.
  • For long joints, weld in short sections and alternate sides to limit distortion.
  • Chip slag and brush between runs.

Inspecting the weld

A good weld has even ripples, the right width, full fusion at both edges and no cracks, holes or undercut. Common faults and causes:

FaultLikely cause
Porosity (holes)Dirty metal, damp electrodes, no gas
UndercutCurrent too high, wrong angle
Lack of fusionCurrent too low, travel too fast
Slag inclusionsSlag not cleaned between runs

lessons.title: Cutting, brazing and soldering in practice
lessons.html:
Oxy-fuel cutting

  1. Check cylinders are chained, regulators and flashback arrestors fitted and hoses in good condition.
  2. Set pressures from the equipment chart for the tip size.
  3. Light the acetylene with a spark lighter, add oxygen to get a neutral preheat flame.
  4. Heat the start point until bright red, then press the cutting oxygen lever.
  5. Move steadily along the line. Too fast and the cut stops; too slow and the edge melts.
  6. Support the work so the off-cut falls safely, away from feet and hoses.

Plasma cutters are also common in workshops and cut stainless steel and aluminium as well as mild steel. Follow the machine's instructions.

Brazing

Brazing is useful for cast iron brackets, thin sheet and joining different metals. Clean the joint, apply flux, heat both parts evenly with the torch until the flux runs clear, and feed the brazing rod so it flows into the joint. Do not overheat. Let the part cool slowly, then clean off flux residue. Do not braze high-stress parts.

Soldering

For wiring repairs: strip the insulation, slide heat-shrink onto the wire, twist or crimp the wires, heat the joint with the iron and apply rosin-core solder to the wire, not the iron. A good joint is shiny and smooth. Slide the heat-shrink over and shrink it. Never use acid flux on electrical work.

Hot-work safety

  • Wear the right PPE: welding helmet with correct shade, leather gloves, apron, safety boots, and goggles for gas work.
  • Clear flammables: chaff, dry grass, oily rags, fuel cans. Farm workshops often have hay and dust nearby.
  • Never weld or cut on fuel tanks or drums unless they have been made safe by a correct procedure.
  • Use screens to protect others from arc flash.
  • Ventilate to remove fumes, especially from galvanised or painted metal.
  • Keep a fire extinguisher at hand and check the area for smouldering for some time after work.
  • Keep cables and hoses dry and undamaged.

Key points

  • Decide whether a part may be welded; never weld ROPS or steering parts.
  • Clean to bright metal and stop cracks with drilled holes.
  • Test settings on scrap and inspect every weld for defects.
  • Braze for cast iron and thin parts, not high-stress parts.
  • Clear flammables and watch for fire after hot work.
